clue.text: Class hosting university meeting

indicators.note: a host has a guest inside the house, so the first word holds the second within it

blocks.note: a form is a school class
U is the standard abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: A school class puts on a gathering at a university.
explanation.definitionFit: A forum is a public gathering or assembly where ideas are discussed, so it is a kind of meeting.

clue.text: Where night-time photography seen instantly?

blocks.note: first meaning: pictures taken in the dark are lit by a burst from the camera's lamp
second meaning: an idiom for something happening very quickly

explanation.walkthrough: The first half is a playful literal reading of the idiom: dark scenes show up only when the camera's bulb fires.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an idiom for immediately, in no time at all, and literally describes photos lit by the camera's bulb.

clue.text: Person installing equipment in better shape

blocks.note: first meaning: a tradesperson who puts in machinery or kitchens
second meaning: the comparative of the adjective for healthy

explanation.surface: An installer who is healthier than before.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun names a tradesperson who assembles machinery; the comparative adjective means healthier, more athletic.

clue.text: Irish playwright certain to get heard?

indicators.note: what is heard is spoken, so the word is judged by its sound rather than its spelling

blocks.note: certain means sure, which in a non-rhotic British accent sounds like the playwright's name

explanation.surface: An Irish dramatist is sure to win an audience.
explanation.walkthrough: The pun works in southern British speech, where the final r is not pronounced and sure rhymes with saw.
explanation.definitionFit: George Bernard Shaw was a Dublin-born dramatist who wrote Pygmalion and Saint Joan.

clue.text: Takeaway favourite passed around a square

indicators.note: something passed around encircles what follows, so the first word wraps the next

blocks.note: a popular delivered meal
taken as written

explanation.surface: A favourite takeaway meal is handed round in a town square.
explanation.definitionFit: A piazza is the Italian name for an open public plaza in a town, used in English too.

clue.text: Fruit in lemon, gone off

indicators.note: food that has gone off is spoiled, so the letters are broken up and rearranged

blocks.note: the letters of both words

explanation.surface: A spoilt piece of fruit inside a lemon that has gone bad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fruit in lemon' reads as one phrase, but 'in' only links the definition to the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: An Ogen is a small sweet variety of cantaloupe developed in Israel, a kind of fruit.

clue.text: Extraordinary thing, word complete

indicators.note: extraordinary means out of the usual order, so the letters are arranged differently

blocks.note: the letters of both words

explanation.surface: An amazing object, a word that is whole.
explanation.definitionFit: As an adjective it means utter or absolute, as in a downright lie, so it is a synonym of total.

clue.text: Noise and energy: wild animal!

blocks.note: a din is a loud noise
go means energy or drive

explanation.surface: A loud, energetic wild creature makes its presence felt.
explanation.definitionFit: The dingo is a feral dog native to Australia, an untamed beast of the outback.

clue.text: Very competitive in the end entering car race

indicators.note: at the end points to the final letter of the word before it
to enter is to go inside, so one piece is placed within the other

blocks.note: a rally is a motor race over public roads
the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: Things get very competitive at the finish of a motor race.
explanation.definitionFit: As an intensifier it works like truly or extremely, as in really good.

clue.text: Batter in self-service selection of meals

blocks.note: first meaning: to strike repeatedly, as wind does a ship
second meaning: a spread of food from which diners help themselves

explanation.surface: Batter, as in pancake mix, served at a help-yourself spread.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Batter' looks like cooking mixture beside the food, but it is the verb meaning to pound.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means to pound or knock about; as a noun, a meal laid out for guests to serve themselves.

clue.text: Struggling for breath, whoopee vitality!

blocks.note: both are cries of delight
zing means liveliness or zest

explanation.surface: Someone gasping for air after an exuberant burst of energy.
explanation.definitionFit: To wheeze is to breathe with a whistling rasp, as asthmatics do when short of air.

clue.text: Mimic standard drivel

blocks.note: par is the normal or expected level
rot means nonsense

explanation.surface: Copying the usual nonsense.
explanation.definitionFit: To parrot is to repeat words without understanding, as the talking bird does, so it means imitate.

clue.text: Note shot in the arm

blocks.note: first meaning: the keynote, first degree of a musical scale
second meaning: something that revives or invigorates

explanation.surface: A memo about receiving an injection.
explanation.definitionFit: In music it is the home pitch of a key; it is also a restorative boost, like a reviving medicine.

clue.text: Shoe for sale, shilling off, tatty

indicators.note: taking something off removes it, so that letter is dropped from the phrase
something tatty is ragged and in disarray, so the remaining letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
s is the old abbreviation for a shilling, a pre-decimal British coin

explanation.surface: A shabby shoe on sale, reduced by a shilling.
explanation.walkthrough: The shilling was a British coin worth twelve old pence; its abbreviation s comes from the Latin solidus.
explanation.definitionFit: A loafer is a laceless slip-on leather shoe, a casual style of footwear.

clue.text: Revealing experience, I said, key?

indicators.note: said means spoken, so the pronoun is replaced by a word sounding the same

blocks.note: the pronoun and the organ of sight sound alike
a key is something that unlocks a door

explanation.surface: Someone recounting an enlightening moment, asking whether it was the crucial one.
explanation.definitionFit: An eye-opener is a surprising event that brings a startling realisation or new understanding.

clue.text: Fairy tale with a little slimy thing

indicators.note: a little of something is only part of it, so the letters sit inside the following words

blocks.note: the letters run across the two words

explanation.surface: A fairy story featuring a small slimy creature, like a frog prince.
explanation.definitionFit: A myth is a traditional story or legend, often of gods or fantastic beings, much like a fable.

clue.text: Gift from the workers, my dear

blocks.note: first meaning: what worker bees produce
second meaning: an affectionate term of address

explanation.surface: A colleague receives a present from the staff and is called dear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Workers' suggests employees; here they are worker bees in a hive.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the sweet syrup bees make from nectar and also an endearment like sweetheart or darling.

clue.text: Marker underlining first of howlers in school

indicators.note: first of points to the opening letter of the word that follows
in a down clue something underlining sits below, so the first piece goes above the second

blocks.note: the opening letter of the word
an arrow is a sign marking a direction

explanation.surface: A teacher's pen marks underlining the mistakes of a pupil.
explanation.walkthrough: Harrow is a famous English private boarding school in north-west London; howlers are blunders in schoolwork.
explanation.definitionFit: Harrow School is one of England's best-known independent schools, so it is an example of a school.

clue.text: Jumper knitted for grandson, originally

indicators.note: knitting loops yarn into a new form, so these letters are worked into a different order
originally means at the start, taking only the opening letter of the word

blocks.note: taken as written
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A grandmother knits a sweater for her grandson.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jumper' is the British word for a sweater, which suits the knitting; here it means a leaping creature.
explanation.definitionFit: A frog is an amphibian famous for leaping, so it is cryptically something that jumps.

clue.text: Time, in making a run for it, passing swiftly

indicators.note: in places the first piece inside the phrase that follows it

blocks.note: running away from danger
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Time slips away quickly while someone runs off.
explanation.definitionFit: Fleeting describes something brief and transient, gone almost as soon as it arrives.

clue.text: An element of the police force?

definitions.text: An element of the police force?

blocks.clueFragment: An element of the police force?
blocks.note: surface reading: one member of the constabulary, a police officer
setter's reading: a chemical element, the metal with symbol Cu, which is also slang for a policeman

explanation.walkthrough: 'Element' reads as 'part' or 'member', but the answer is also an actual metallic element; a copper is British slang for a police officer.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is informal British slang for a police officer and also names the reddish metal on the periodic table.

clue.text: Rather lovely

blocks.note: first meaning: fairly or quite, as an adverb
second meaning: attractive to look at

explanation.surface: Something quite charming.
explanation.definitionFit: As an adverb it means fairly or somewhat, as in pretty good; as an adjective it means attractive.

clue.text: Beauty, one sealing bottle?

blocks.note: first meaning: an outstanding person or thing
second meaning: playfully, someone who puts stoppers into bottles

explanation.surface: A lovely person working on a bottling line.
explanation.walkthrough: The second meaning is a whimsical coinage, signalled by the question mark: a person who stoppers bottles.
explanation.definitionFit: Informally, a corker is something or someone excellent or striking, a real stunner.

clue.text: Savour flavour!

blocks.note: first meaning: to enjoy greatly, as a verb
second meaning: taste or zest, as a noun

explanation.surface: A cook urging someone to enjoy the taste.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means to enjoy with gusto; as a noun it means a distinctive taste or a tangy condiment.

clue.text: Stoop when Hamlet, say, mentioned?

indicators.note: something mentioned is spoken aloud, so the word is chosen for its sound

blocks.note: Hamlet was a prince of Denmark, an example of a Dane

explanation.surface: An actor asks whether to bend down when Hamlet is named.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hamlet' tempts as a small village, but 'say' marks him as one example of a Dane, the Danish prince.
explanation.definitionFit: To deign is to condescend, lowering oneself to do something thought beneath one's dignity.

clue.text: Monster plant brought back by you and I

indicators.note: brought back means returned, so the word is read from end to start

blocks.note: the first-person plural pronoun
a flower is a blooming plant

explanation.surface: Two people bring home a monstrous plant.
explanation.definitionFit: A werewolf is a legendary person who turns into a wolf at full moon, a creature of horror.

clue.text: New-born animal, filly’s offspring appearing little, first of all

indicators.note: first of all takes the opening letter of every one of the preceding words

blocks.note: the initials of the four words

explanation.surface: A newborn horse, the young of a filly, looks small at first.
explanation.definitionFit: A foal is a young horse or donkey, typically under a year old, so it is a baby animal.

clue.text: Second dish, no starter

indicators.note: no starter means the word loses its opening letter

blocks.note: a platter is a large serving plate

explanation.surface: A main course follows, with no appetiser served first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Starter' looks like part of the meal theme, but it marks dropping the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Of two things mentioned, the latter is the one named after the other, the last of a pair.

clue.text: Cheeky youth’s back in Scottish city

indicators.note: the back of a word is its final letter, the only one kept here

blocks.note: pert means impudent
the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: An impudent young person returns to a Scottish town.
explanation.definitionFit: Perth is a city on the River Tay in central Scotland, once its royal capital.

clue.text: Crime concealed by attendant where parish priest lives

indicators.note: something concealed by another is hidden inside it, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: a page is a young attendant or servant
arson is the crime of setting fires deliberately

explanation.surface: An offence covered up by a servant at the vicar's home.
explanation.definitionFit: A parsonage is the house provided by the church for a parson, a clergyman's official residence.
